claim: Breast cancer is the most prevalent malignancy in women and its incidence is increasing globally, especially in developed countries.
source: Breast cancer is the most prevalent malignancy in women and its incidence is increasing globally, especially in developed countries (Bianchini et al., 2016; Siegel et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bianchini et al., 2016; Siegel et al., 2020).

claim: Different treatment strategies, such as surgical resection, hormone therapy, targeted therapy, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, have greatly improved survival of breast cancer patients.
source: Different treatment strategies, such as surgical resection, hormone therapy, targeted therapy, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, have greatly improved survival of breast cancer patients (Bray et al., 2018; Burstein et al., 2014; Early Breast Cancer Trialists' Collaborative G, 2015; Khan et al., 2012; Saini et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Continuous treatment with tamoxifen for 10 years has reduced cancer recurrence and mortality of patients with luminal A breast cancer.
source: Although continuous treatment with tamoxifen for 10 years has reduced cancer recurrence and mortality of patients with luminal A breast cancer, a significant proportion of patients may be over-treated (Bianchini et al., 2016; O'Conor et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bianchini et al., 2016; O'Conor et al., 2018).

claim: Delayed breast cancer metastasis can occur even 20–40 years after breast cancer diagnosis.
source: Furthermore, the available therapies can also lead to a considerable number of patients at a risk to develop a delayed breast cancer metastasis, which occurs even 20–40 years after breast cancer diagnosis (Sharma, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Sharma, 2018).

claim: Breast cancer metastasis occurring 5–8 years after initial surgical resection has become a significant cause of cancer relapse, progression, and poor survival in patients.
source: Notably, breast cancer metastasis occurring 5–8 years after initial surgical resection has become a significant cause of cancer relapse, progression, and poor survival in patients (Nishimura et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Nishimura et al., 2013).

claim: Tumor metastasis is a multistep process during which cancer cells escape from the primary site, migrate into neighboring or distant tissues, extravasate, survive, and colonize, leading to the formation of new tumor nodules at a secondary site.
source: Indeed, tumor metastasis is a multistep process, during which, cancer cells escape from the primary site, migration into a neighboring or distant tissues, extravasation, survival, and colonization, leading to the formation of new tumor nodules at a secondary site (Drabsch and ten Dijke, 2011; Klein, 2008; Scott et al., 2012; Syn et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The rate-limiting step of cancer metastasis is cancer cell colonization and proliferation at the secondary site.
source: The rate-limiting step of cancer metastasis is cancer cell colonization and proliferation at the secondary site, because the initial metastatic cancer nodule usually lacks an efficient vasculature to provide sufficient nutrients to support cancer cell growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by logical inference from the explanation provided about vasculature and nutrient supply.

claim: CD44+/CD24- breast cancer cells from primary breast tumors are associated with distant metastasis.
source: Molecularly, CD44+/CD24- breast cancer cells from primary breast tumors are associated with distant metastasis (Abraham et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Abraham et al., 2005).

claim: CD44+/CD24- breast cancer cells display potent motility and invasiveness.
source: and these cells display potent motility and invasiveness (Liu et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Liu et al., 2010).

claim: CD44+/CD24- breast cancer cells are similar to chemoresistance cancer stem cells (CSCs).
source: similar to chemoresistance cancer stem cells (CSCs) (Velasco-Velázquez et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Velasco-Velázquez et al., 2011).

claim: CD44+/CD24- breast CSCs may be a dominant factor for the relapse of triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), due to their potent self-renewal and differentiation capacities.
source: Previous studies have shown that CD44+/CD24- breast CSCs may be a dominant factor for the relapse of triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), due to their potent self-renewal and differentiation capacities (Geng et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Geng et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014).

claim: Injection with about 50 breast CSCs can induce a solid tumor mass in immunocompromised mice.
source: Indeed, injection with about 50 breast CSCs can induce a solid tumor mass in immunocompromised mice (Chaffer et al., 2011; Iliopoulos et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chaffer et al., 2011; Iliopoulos et al., 2011).

claim: Breast CSCs are commonly prone to be resistant to chemotherapy.
source: Thus, the number of breast CSCs in the secondary site may affect the efficient formation of early metastatic nodules, and breast CSCs are commonly prone to be resistant to chemotherapy (De Angelis et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (De Angelis et al., 2019).

claim: Differentiated cancer cells can spontaneously convert into CSCs to renew the CSC pool in breast cancer, pancreatic cancer and sarcomas, resulting in chemoresistance.
source: Moreover, previous studies have reported that the differentiated cancer cells can spontaneously convert into CSCs to renew the CSC pool in breast cancer, pancreatic cancer and sarcomas, resulting in chemoresistance (Gruber et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015; Ye et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gruber et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015; Ye et al., 2018).

claim: The frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells in human tumor specimens may be useful in the prediction of delayed breast cancer metastasis.
source: Accordingly, it is reasonable to hypothesize that the frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells in human tumor specimens may be useful in the prediction of delayed breast cancer metastasis.
evidence: The claim is presented as a hypothesis based on logical inference from previous observations.

claim: Paraffin-embedded surgical tissue samples were collected from 576 breast cancer patients who underwent breast cancer surgery between June 2005 and April 2013.
source: Paraffin-embedded surgical tissue samples were collected from 576 breast cancer patients, who underwent breast cancer surgery between June 2005 and April 2013 in China Medical University Affiliated Hospital (Shenyang, Liaoning, China), Liaoning Cancer Hospital (Shenyang, Liaoning, China), and Dalian Municipal Central Hospital Affiliated to Dalian Medical University (Dalian, Liaoning, China).
evidence: The claim describes the data collection methodology used in the study.

claim: The frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells in breast cancer tissues of patients with postoperative distant metastasis was significantly higher than those without distant metastasis (p<0.0001).
source: After stratification of the training group of patients, based on their distant metastasis, the frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells in breast cancer tissues of patients with postoperative distant metastasis was significantly higher than those without distant metastasis (p<0.0001; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The ROC analysis revealed a cut-off value of 19.5% with a sensitivity of 70.5%, specificity of 71.2% and Youden index of 0.471.
source: The ROC analysis revealed a cut-off value of 19.5% with a sensitivity of 70.5%, specificity of 71.2% and Youden index of 0.471 (Figure 1B; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC analysis data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: In the training set of patients, the metastasis rate in the patients with a high frequency (>19.5%) of CD44-/CD24- breast cancer cells was 1.97-fold higher than those with a low frequency (<19.5%) of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells.
source: In the training set of patients, the metastasis rate in the patients with a high frequency (>19.5%) of CD44-/CD24- breast cancer cells was 1.97-fold higher than those with a low frequency (<19.5%) of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis from the training set of patients.

claim: The metastatic rates in the patients with a high frequency of CD44-/CD24- breast cancer cells were significantly higher than those with a low frequency of this type of cells (i.e. 40.85% vs. 6.82% for luminal; 47.06% vs. 13.64% for HER-2+; 63.79% vs. 22.22% for TNBC with a high vs. low frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells).
source: Analysis of different molecular subtypes of breast cancers indicated that the metastatic rates in the patients with a high frequency of CD44-/CD24- breast cancer cells were significantly higher than those with a low frequency of this type of cells (i.e. 40.85% vs. 6.82% for luminal; 47.06% vs. 13.64% for HER-2+; 63.79% vs. 22.22% for TNBC with a high vs. low frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells; Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: High frequency of CD44-/CD24- cancer cells or CSCs, positive lymph node metastasis, higher N stage, and TNBC were independent risk factors for poor DFS.
source: Univariate and multivariate analyses indicated that high frequency of CD44-/CD24- cancer cells or CSCs, positive lymph node metastasis, higher N stage, and TNBC were independent risk factors for poor DFS (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by univariate and multivariate statistical analyses presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: CD44-/CD24- TNBC cells spontaneously converted into CD44+/CD24- CSCs in vitro.
source: Subsequently, CD44-/CD24- cells were cultured for 7 days. There were 4.6% of CD44+/CD24- CSCs (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing conversion after 7 days of culture, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Following implantation with CD44-/CD24- MDA-MB-231 cells in the breast fat pad of female BALB/c nude mice, 10.8–16.3% of CD44+/CD24- CSCs were detected in the formed tumors at 7 and 21 days post implantation in mice, respectively.
source: Following implantation with CD44-/CD24- MDA-MB-231 cells in the breast fat pad of female BALB/c nude mice, 10.8–16.3% of CD44+/CD24- CSCs were detected in the formed tumors at 7 and 21 days post implantation in mice, respectively (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Following culture of CD44-/CD24- cells from MDA-MB-231 cells, flow cytometry analysis exhibited 28.3% and 24.7% of CD44+/CD24- cells in SC and L15 media, respectively.
source: Following culture of CD44-/CD24- cells from MDA-MB-231 cells, flow cytometry analysis exhibited 28.3% and 24.7% of CD44+/CD24- cells in SC and L15 media, respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Both WT CSCs and CD44-/CD24- CSCs formed similar numbers of mammospheres with comparable sizes.
source: Both WT CSCs and CD44-/CD24- CSCs formed similar numbers of mammospheres with comparable sizes (Figure 4A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both WT CSCs and CD44-/CD24- CSCs displayed similar proliferative capacity.
source: and displayed similar proliferative capacity (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Culture of both types of CSCs for 7 days promoted their differentiation into different subtypes of MDA-MB-231 cells with similar percentages.
source: Culture of both types of CSCs for 7 days promoted their differentiation into different subtypes of MDA-MB-231 cells with similar percentages (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: The relative levels of OCT4, SOX2, NANOG, NESTIN, and ABCB1 proteins were comparable between WT CSCs and CD44-/CD24- CSCs.
source: Western blot analysis revealed that the relative levels of OCT4, SOX2, NANOG, NESTIN, and ABCB1 proteins were also comparable between these two types of CSCs (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Both WT CSCs and CD44-/CD24- CSCs induced xenograft tumors with similar sizes and weights after implantation for 21 days.
source: After implantation with the same number of each type of CSCs for 21 days, both types of CSCs induced xenograft tumors with similar sizes and weights (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Intravenous injection of equal number of each type of CSCs induced lung metastatic nodules with similar tumor sizes and lung weights in NOD/SCID mice.
source: Furthermore, intravenous injection of equal number of each type of CSCs induced lung metastatic nodules with similar tumor sizes and lung weights in NOD/SCID mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: RNA-seq analysis identified 11 DEGs associated with tumor cell differentiation and dedifferentiation between EGFP- CD44-/CD24- cells and EGFP+ CSCs, including RHBDL2, HIST1H4H, DSCC1, ZNF710, ATP8B3, and others.
source: There were 11 DEGs associated with tumor cell differentiation and dedifferentiation between EGFP- CD44-/CD24- cells and EGFP+ CSCs and they included RHBDL2, HIST1H4H, DSCC1, ZNF710, ATP8B3, and others.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis data.

claim: Comparison of EGFP+ CSCs (120 hr post culture) with EGFP- (24 hr post culture) and uncommitted cells (72 hr post culture) revealed that both RHBDL2 and HIST1H4H mRNA transcripts significantly increased.
source: Particularly, comparison of EGFP+ CSCs (120 hr post culture) with EGFP- (24 hr post culture) and uncommitted cells (72 hr post culture) revealed that both RHBDL2 and HIST1H4H mRNA transcripts significantly increased (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Higher levels of HIST1H4H, RHBDL2, DSCC1, ARL6IP1, PPME1, and lower levels of G2E3 and MED22 mRNA transcripts were significantly associated with worse DFS in breast cancer patients in the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database.
source: Furthermore, Kaplan-Meier analysis and log-rank test indicated that higher levels of HIST1H4H, RHBDL2, DSCC1, ARL6IP1, PPME1, and lower levels of G2E3 and MED22 mRNA transcripts, but not others, were significantly associated with worse DFS in breast cancer patients in the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Compared with the unconverted CD44-/CD24- tumor cells, PPME1, RHBDL2 and HIST1H4H mRNA transcripts increased in the newly converted CD44+/CD24- CSCs with a change of >two folds, which were similar to that in parental CD44+/CD24- CSCs.
source: Compared with the unconverted CD44-/CD24- tumor cells, PPME1, RHBDL2 and HIST1H4H mRNA transcripts increased in the newly converted CD44+/CD24- CSCs with a change of >two folds, which were similar to that in parental CD44+/CD24- CSCs (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: RHBDL2 silencing dramatically decreased RHBDL2 and YAP1 expression and slightly increased YAP1 phosphorylation in both TNBC cells.
source: Compared with the controls, RHBDL2 silencing dramatically decreased RHBDL2 and YAP1 expression and slightly increased YAP1 phosphorylation in both TNBC cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: RHBDL2 silencing obviously increased the relative levels of USP31 expression, YAP1 phosphorylation and decreased the relative levels of NF-kB phosphorylation in CD44-/CD24- cells sorted from both the negative control (NC) and RHBDL2-silenced MDA-MB-231 cells and MDA-MB-468 cells.
source: Furthermore, RHBDL2 silencing also obviously increased the relative levels of USP31 expression, YAP1 phosphorylation and decreased the relative levels of NF-kB phosphorylation, besides the demolished RHBDL2 expression, in CD44-/CD24- cells sorted from both the negative control (NC) and RHBDL2-silenced MDA-MB-231 cells and MDA-MB-468 cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: RHBDL2 silencing not only decreased YAP1 expression in the cytoplasm, but also dramatically reduced the levels of nuclear YAP1 in both TNBC cells.
source: Moreover, RHBDL2 silencing not only decreased YAP1 expression in the cytoplasm, but also dramatically reduced the levels of nuclear YAP1 in both TNBC cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data of cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions shown in Figure 7C.

claim: RHBDL2 silencing remarkably decreased the percentages of CD44+/CD24- CSCs from 6.5–5.5% to 0.5–0.7% in both types of TNBC cells.
source: In addition, after culture of control CD44-/CD24- and RHBDL2-silenced CD44-/CD24- cells in L15 medium for 7 days, the results indicated that RHBDL2 silencing remarkably decreased the percentages of CD44+/CD24- CSCs from 6.5–5.5% to 0.5–0.7% in both types of TNBC cells (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 7D and 7E.

claim: RHBDL2 silencing significantly decreased the numbers and sizes of formed mammospheres in both types of TNBC cells.
source: Compared with the control siRNA-transfected cells, RHBDL2 silencing significantly decreased the numbers and sizes of formed mammospheres in both types of TNBC cells (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by mammosphere formation assay data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: A higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells in breast cancer tissues was associated with significantly with worse DFS and delayed distant metastasis.
source: More importantly, a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells in breast cancer tissues was associated with significantly with worse DFS and delayed distant metastasis.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis from the study.

claim: RHBDL2 may be a crucial regulator of the spontaneous conversion of CD44-/CD24- TNBC cells into CD44+/CD24- CSCs by enhancing the YAP1/USP31/NF-κB signaling in breast cancer cells.
source: Therefore, these findings further suggest that RHBDL2 may be a crucial regulator of the spontaneous conversion of CD44-/CD24- TNBC cells into CD44+/CD24- CSCs by enhancing the YAP1/USP31/NF-κB signaling in breast cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing RHBDL2 silencing effects on YAP1/USP31/NF-κB signaling and CSC conversion.

claim: The frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells and RHBDL2 may be valuable for prognosis of delayed breast cancer metastasis, particularly for TNBC.
source: These findings suggest that the frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells and RHBDL2 may be valuable for prognosis of delayed breast cancer metastasis, particularly for TNBC.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study findings.

claim: Non-CSC tumor cells can dedifferentiate (convert) into CSCs in human glioblastoma and intestinal stroma melanoma, contributing to intra- and inter-tumor heterogeneity.
source: Previous studies have shown that non-CSC tumor cells can dedifferentiate (convert) into CSCs in human glioblastoma and intestinal stroma melanoma, contributing to intra- and inter-tumor heterogeneity (Stepanova et al., 2003; Tzimas et al., 2006; Wei et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Stepanova et al., 2003; Tzimas et al., 2006; Wei et al., 2019).

claim: CSC plasticity and heterogeneity can promote tumor progression and resistance to therapy.
source: Furthermore, CSC plasticity and heterogeneity can promote tumor progression and resistance to therapy (Das et al., 2020; Kilmister et al., 2020; Martin-Castillo et al., 2013; Thankamony et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Das et al., 2020; Kilmister et al., 2020; Martin-Castillo et al., 2013; Thankamony et al., 2020).

claim: Intra-tumoral heterogeneity is a major ongoing challenge for effective cancer therapy.
source: For example, intra-tumoral heterogeneity is a major ongoing challenge for effective cancer therapy, while CSCs are responsible for intra-tumoral heterogeneity, therapeutic resistance, and metastasis, which may be because cancer cells exhibit a high level of plasticity and an ability to dynamically switch between CSC and non-CSC states or among different subsets of CSCs (Thankamony et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Thankamony et al., 2020).

claim: The differentiated non-CSCs can revert to be trastuzumab-refractory, CSS-like cells by enhancing their epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition process.
source: Consistently, the differentiated non-CSCs can revert to be trastuzumab-refractory, CSS-like cells by enhancing their epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition process (Martin-Castillo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Martin-Castillo et al., 2013).

claim: The changes in tumor microenvironment and epigenetics can promote the conversion of non-CSCs into CSCs, leading to tumor progression and therapeutic resistance.
source: Similarly, the changes in tumor microenvironment and epigenetics can promote the conversion of non-CSCs into CSCs, leading to tumor progression and therapeutic resistance (Das et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Das et al., 2020).

claim: The higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells effectively predicted delayed distant metastasis in cases with a low frequency of CSCs.
source: Particularly, the higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cancer cells was a better predictor of delayed breast cancer metastasis (up to 12 years after initial breast cancer diagnosis). Evidently, while high frequency of CSCs was valuable for predicting distant metastasis at 5–7 years post-surgery a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells effectively predicted delayed distant metastasis in cases with a low frequency of CSCs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study findings.

claim: RHBDL2, also known as the rhomboid like 2, is one intramembrane serine protease of the secretase-A rhomboid family.
source: The RHBDL2, also known as the rhomboid like 2, is one intramembrane serine protease of the secretase-A rhomboid family (Etheridge et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Etheridge et al., 2013).

claim: RHBDL2 cleaves its substrates, including EGF, ephrin-β3, thrombomodulin, the C-type lectin family 14 member A (CLEC14A), cadherin, IL-6R, Spint-1 and the collagen receptor tyrosine kinase DDR1.
source: Previous studies have identified that the RHBDL2 cleaves its substrates, including EGF, ephrin-β3, thrombomodulin, the C-type lectin family 14 member A (CLEC14A), cadherin, IL-6R, Spint-1 and the collagen receptor tyrosine kinase DDR1 (Adrain et al., 2011; Battistini et al., 2019; Etheridge et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Adrain et al., 2011; Battistini et al., 2019; Etheridge et al., 2013).

claim: RHBDL2 functionally activates the EGF signaling, cadherin shedding, angiogenesis and promotes the wound healing and migration of different types of cells, including tumor cells.
source: Although the functional consequence of cleaving these substrates has not been fully explored the available findings indicate that RHBDL2 functionally activates the EGF signaling, cadherin shedding, angiogenesis and promotes the wound healing and migration of different types of cells, including tumor cells (Adrain et al., 2011; Cheng et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Adrain et al., 2011; Cheng et al., 2011).

claim: Up-regulated RHBDL2 expression is associated with worse prognosis of several types of malignant tumors, such as breast cancer, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, clear cell kidney cancer, and low-grade glioma patient.
source: Furthermore, up-regulated RHBDL2 expression is associated with worse prognosis of several types of malignant tumors, such as breast cancer, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, clear cell kidney cancer, and low-grade glioma patient (Canzoneri et al., 2014; Johnson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Canzoneri et al., 2014; Johnson et al., 2017).

claim: YAP1 can enhance CSC stemness in several types of human cancers.
source: YAP1 can enhance CSC stemness in several types of human cancers, and aberrant YAP1 activation is associated with a low level of TNBC differentiation and poor survival of breast cancer patients (Bora-Singhal et al., 2015; Hansen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bora-Singhal et al., 2015; Hansen et al., 2015).

claim: Aberrant YAP1 activation is associated with a low level of TNBC differentiation and poor survival of breast cancer patients.
source: YAP1 can enhance CSC stemness in several types of human cancers, and aberrant YAP1 activation is associated with a low level of TNBC differentiation and poor survival of breast cancer patients (Bora-Singhal et al., 2015; Hansen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bora-Singhal et al., 2015; Hansen et al., 2015).

claim: RHBDL2 promoted the spontaneous conversion of CD44-/CD24- cells into CD44+/CD24- CSCs by enhancing YAP1 stability through inhibiting its phosphorylation to suppress USP31 expression, enhancing the NF-κB signaling in breast cancer cells.
source: Therefore, the findings from the current study indicated that RHBDL2 promoted the spontaneous conversion of CD44-/CD24- cells into CD44+/CD24- CSCs by enhancing YAP1 stability through inhibiting its phosphorylation to suppress USP31 expression, enhancing the NF-κB signaling in breast cancer cells, whereas RHBDL2 silencing had the opposite effects in breast cancer cells (Figure 7G).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results and is illustrated in Figure 7G.

claim: RHBDL2 may cleave other substrates to activate the EGF receptor-mediated signaling, and modify cadherin and other molecules through their involved signal pathways to promote the spontaneous conversion of CD44-/CD24- cells into CD44+/CD24- CSCs.
source: Alternatively, RHBDL2 may cleave other substrates to activate the EGF receptor-mediated signaling, and modify cadherin and other molecules through their involved signal pathways to promote the spontaneous conversion of CD44-/CD24- cells into CD44+/CD24- CSCs.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing alternative mechanisms based on known RHBDL2 functions.

claim: RHBDL2 may be a new therapeutic target for control of CD44-/CD24- cell conversion into CSCs to reduce CSC pool size and limit breast cancer progression and metastasis.
source: Given that CSCs are crucial for breast cancer progression and metastasis, RHBDL2 may be a new therapeutic target for control of CD44-/CD24- cell conversion into CSCs to reduce CSC pool size and limit breast cancer progression and metastasis.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing RHBDL2 as a therapeutic target based on the study findings.

claim: Patients with a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells in their breast cancer tissues had a high risk to develop delayed distant metastasis 5–7 years after diagnosis.
source: In summary, postoperative breast cancer metastasis, especially delayed metastasis (e.g. ≥5 years after diagnosis), is an important unresolved issue. The results from the current study indicated that patients with a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells in their breast cancer tissues had a high risk to develop delayed distant metastasis 5–7 years after diagnosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis from the study.

claim: CD44-/CD24- cells spontaneously converted into CD44+/CD24- CSCs and both WT and newly converted CSCs had similar stemness properties in vitro and in vivo.
source: Mechanistically, CD44-/CD24- cells spontaneously converted into CD44+/CD24- CSCs and both WT and newly converted CSCs had similar stemness properties in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: RHBDL2 silencing significantly decreased YAP1 expression and increased USP31 expression to attenuate the NF-kB activation and CD44-/CD24- cell conversion into CSCs as well as their mammosphere formation.
source: RHBDL2 silencing significantly decreased YAP1 expression and increased USP31 expression to attenuate the NF-kB activation and CD44-/CD24- cell conversion into CSCs as well as their mammosphere formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: RHBDL2 may act as a positive regulator of the spontaneous conversion of CD44-/CD24- cells into CSCs by enhancing the YAP1/USP31/NF-kB signaling.
source: RHBDL2 may act as a positive regulator of the spontaneous conversion of CD44-/CD24- cells into CSCs by enhancing the YAP1/USP31/NF-kB signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Higher frequency (≥19.5%) of CD44-/CD24- cells was associated with delayed postoperative breast cancer metastasis.
source: The results indicated that higher frequency (≥19.5%) of CD44-/CD24- cells was associated with delayed postoperative breast cancer metastasis.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis from the study.

claim: CD44-/CD24-triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) cells spontaneously converted into CD44+/CD24-cancer stem cells (CSCs) with properties similar to CD44+/CD24-CSCs from primary human breast cancer cells and parental TNBC cells in terms of stemness marker expression, self-renewal, differentiation, tumorigenicity, and lung metastasis in vitro and in NOD/SCID mice.
source: Furthermore, CD44-/CD24-triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) cells spontaneously converted into CD44+/CD24-cancer stem cells (CSCs) with properties similar to CD44+/CD24-CSCs from primary human breast cancer cells and parental TNBC cells in terms of stemness marker expression, self-renewal, differentiation, tumorigenicity, and lung metastasis in vitro and in NOD/SCID mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: RNA sequencing identified several differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in newly converted CSCs and RHBDL2, one of the DEGs, expression was upregulated.
source: RNA sequencing identified several differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in newly converted CSCs and RHBDL2, one of the DEGs, expression was upregulated.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data from the study.

claim: RHBDL2 silencing inhibited the YAP1/USP31/NF-κB signaling and attenuated spontaneous CD44-/CD24- cell conversion into CSCs and their mammosphere formation.
source: More importantly, RHBDL2 silencing inhibited the YAP1/USP31/NF-κB signaling and attenuated spontaneous CD44-/CD24- cell conversion into CSCs and their mammosphere formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The average frequency of CD44-/CD24- cancer cells in all samples was 19.7% with a median value of 19.5%.
source: The average frequency of CD44-/CD24- cancer cells in all samples was 19.7% with a median value of 19.5%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis from the study.

claim: Patients with a higher frequency (≥2%) of CD44+/CD24- CSCs usually developed distant metastasis earlier than those with < 2% of CD44+/CD24- and >19.5% of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells.
source: Furthermore, analysis of metastatic dynamics revealed that patients with a higher frequency (≥2%) of CD44+/CD24- CSCs usually developed distant metastasis earlier than those with < 2% of CD44+/CD24- and >19.5% of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells (the C1 group, Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The DFS of patients with a high frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells or CD44+/CD24- CSCs was significantly shorter than those with a low frequency of corresponding cells.
source: Similarly, the DFS of patients with a high frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells or CD44+/CD24- CSCs was significantly shorter than those with a low frequency of corresponding cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Patients with a high frequency of CSCs had a metastatic peak near 5 years after surgical resection of the tumor.
source: The metastatic dynamics also indicated that patients with a high frequency of CSCs had a metastatic peak near 5 years after surgical resection of the tumor (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Patients in the C1 group also had a higher risk to develop delayed distant metastasis during 5–7 years post tumor resection than those with <2% of CD44+/CD24- CSCs and < 19.5% of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells (the C0 group).
source: However, to exclude the effects of CSCs, patients in the C1 group also had a higher risk to develop delayed distant metastasis during 5–7 years post tumor resection than those with <2% of CD44+/CD24- CSCs and < 19.5% of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells (the C0 group, Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TNBC and luminal breast cancer patients with a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells had a worse DFS, compared than those with a lower frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells following standard therapies.
source: As shown in Figure 1F and G, TNBC and luminal breast cancer patients with a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells had a worse DFS, compared than those with a lower frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells following standard therapies.
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: A higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- breast cancer cells, like higher frequency of CD44+/CD24- CSCs, was associated significantly with a shorter DFS in the training set of patients regardless of standard therapies.
source: Hence, a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- breast cancer cells, like higher frequency of CD44+/CD24- CSCs, was associated significantly with a shorter DFS in the training set of patients regardless of standard therapies.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis from the study.

claim: The metastatic rates of patients with a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells were higher than those with a lower frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells in the tested molecular subtypes of breast cancers (22.73% vs. 8.89% for luminal; 50% vs. 18.42% for HER-2+; 41.67% vs. 15% for TNBC with high vs. low CD44-/CD24- cells).
source: To validate the importance of CD44-/CD24- cell frequency in delayed metastasis, the testing set of patients was analyzed and the metastatic rates of patients with a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells were higher than those with a lower frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells in the tested molecular subtypes of breast cancers (22.73% vs. 8.89% for luminal; 50% vs. 18.42% for HER-2+; 41.67% vs. 15% for TNBC with high vs. low CD44-/CD24- cells; Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The DFS and OS of patients with a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells were significantly shorter than those with a lower frequency of CD44-/CD24- cell cells in the testing set.
source: The DFS and OS of patients with a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells were significantly shorter than those with a lower frequency of CD44-/CD24- cell cells in the testing set (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: The DFS and OS of patients with a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells were significantly shorter than those with a lower frequency of them, regardless of their molecular subtypes.
source: Similarly, the DFS and OS of patients with a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells were significantly shorter than those with a lower frequency of them, regardless of their molecular subtypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Patients in the C1 group developed delayed distant metastasis, which peaked between 4 and 5 years post tumor resection.
source: The metastatic dynamics revealed that while higher and earlier metastatic rates were observed in the testing set of patients, particularly for those with a high frequency of CD44+/CD24- CSCs and those with < 2% of CD44+/CD24- CSCs and >19.5% of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells in the (C1 group) developed delayed distant metastasis, which peaked between 4 and 5 years post tumor resection (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Following standard chemotherapy or endocrine therapy, the patients with a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells had a significantly shorter DFS than their corresponding patients with a lower frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells.
source: Furthermore, following standard chemotherapy or endocrine therapy, the patients with a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells had a significantly shorter DFS than their corresponding patients with a lower frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: Patients in the C1 group, with a low frequency of CSCs and higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells, also had a worse DFS than those with a lower frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells in the C0 group.
source: Moreover, patients in the C1 group, with a low frequency of CSCs and higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells, also had a worse DFS than those with a lower frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells in the C0 group (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: TNBC patients with a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells had a high risk to develop progressive metastasis at 4 years post tumor resection regardless of chemotherapy.
source: A similar pattern of DFS was observed in TNBC patients and those with a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells had a high risk to develop progressive metastasis at 4 years post tumor resection regardless of chemotherapy (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells in tumor tissues could be a valuable predictor of standard therapeutic response in breast cancer patients.
source: In this regard, the frequency of CD44-/CD24- cells in tumor tissues could be a valuable predictor of standard therapeutic response in breast cancer patients.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study findings.

claim: A higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells was associated with worse survival of breast cancer patients following standard therapies.
source: Thus, a higher frequency of CD44-/CD24- tumor cells was associated with worse survival of breast cancer patients following standard therapies.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis from the study.

claim: There were 4.6% of CD44+/CD24- CSCs after culturing primary human CD44-/CD24- cells for 7 days.
source: Subsequently, CD44-/CD24- cells were cultured for 7 days. There were 4.6% of CD44+/CD24- CSCs (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CD44-/CD24- TNBC cells effectively converted into CD44+/CD24- CSCs in vitro and in vivo.
source: Clearly, CD44-/CD24- TNBC cells effectively converted into CD44+/CD24- CSCs in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Both types of CSCs exhibited comparable capacities to self-renew, differentiate and form mammospheres, and had similar stemness properties.
source: Thus, both types of CSCs exhibited comparable capacities to self-renew, differentiate and form mammospheres, and had similar stemness properties.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Both WT CSCs and CD44-/CD24- CSCs from TNBC cells had similar tumorigenicity and metastatic capacities in vivo.
source: Thus, both WT CSCs and CD44-/CD24- CSCs from TNBC cells had similar tumorigenicity and metastatic capacities in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data from the study.

claim: GO and KEGG analyses revealed that all DEGs were predominantly involved in cell organelle formation, metabolism, signal transduction, and transcriptional regulation.
source: GO and KEGG analyses revealed that all DEGs were predominantly involved in cell organelle formation, metabolism, signal transduction, and transcriptional regulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO and KEGG analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Up-regulated expression of PPME1, RHBDL2 and HIST1H4H may be crucial for the spontaneous conversion of CD44-/CD24- TNBC cells into CD44+/CD24- CSCs.
source: Together, these data suggest that up-regulated expression of these genes may be crucial for the spontaneous conversion of CD44-/CD24- TNBC cells into CD44+/CD24- CSCs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The YAP1 signaling can suppress USP31 expression, a potent inhibitor of the NF-κB signaling.
source: Because the YAP1 signaling can suppress USP31 expression, a potent inhibitor of the NF-κB signaling, how RHBDL2 silencing could affect the relative levels of YAP1 expression and phosphorylation was investigated in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the YAP1/USP31/NF-κB signaling pathway.

claim: The spontaneous conversion of CD44-/CD24- cells helps maintain the CSC pool size, contributing to the delayed distant metastasis and worse prognosis in breast cancer patients.
source: These, together with the dynamic process of spontaneous conversion of non-CSC CD44-/CD24- cells and CSC differentiation, indicate that the spontaneous conversion of CD44-/CD24- cells helps maintain the CSC pool size, contributing to the delayed distant metastasis and worse prognosis in breast cancer patients.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study findings.

claim: CD44-/CD24- cells may spontaneously convert into CSCs and cause delayed distant metastasis when environmental and other factors cause a clonal evolution by accumulating successive mutations.
source: These results suggest that CD44-/CD24- cells may spontaneously convert into CSCs and cause delayed distant metastasis when environmental and other factors cause a clonal evolution by accumulating successive mutations (Meacham and Morrison, 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and supported by a citation to published literature (Meacham and Morrison, 2013).

claim: The upregulated RHBDL2 transcription was associated with worse DFS of breast cancer patients in TCGA.
source: Interestingly, the current study not only observed that the upregulated RHBDL2 transcription was associated with worse DFS of breast cancer patients in TCGA
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TCGA data.

claim: YAP1-mediated suppression of USP31 enhances NF-κB activity to promote sarcomagenesis.
source: Moreover, these data extended previous observation that YAP1-mediated suppression of USP31 enhances NF-κB activity to promote sarcomagenesis (Kemeny and Fisher, 2018; Mehta et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kemeny and Fisher, 2018; Mehta et al., 2018).
